newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialist-Communist win worst bond outcome.
newsitem.headline: French Socialist-Communist win worst bond outcome.

text.p: French capital markets looked set to fall on Monday after a parliamentary election put the opposition Socialists in power, but needing support from the Communist Party.
"The need for Communist support was not priced into the market on Friday," UBS economist Eric Muller said. "It is the worst case scenario."

While in practice the anti-Maastricht Communists would probably support the Socialists on major decisions, the presence of a party in government which wants a referendum on the single currency would increase concerns about the whole project.

"There will be a certain amount of hope that things will go ahead, that the momentum is there and (Socialist party leader Lionel) Jospin isn't going to upset the apple cart," Sonja Gibbs, bond strategist at Nomura International said. "But at the same time people are aware reliance on the Communists will make things harder.

She said a combination of Socialists and Communists was the result which international investors feared most. "The danger factor is if they have to govern with the Communists. It inches the probability from a broad EMU to EMU being in trouble."
Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley, said, "The main reaction will be that all this is bad for core European assets and we are going to see higher long bond yields for everybody."

"I don't know if the (10-year bond yield) spread between France and Germany will move. If the market goes down French investors will buy," he said. "I expect the currency to be under pressure and of course the short end of the market."
"The initial reaction may be to dump Europe altogether -- then in a few weeks if EMU is still in jeopardy, if the German government continues to tear itself apart, I would buy the mark," Gibbs said.

Jean-Francois Mercier, economist at Salomon Brothers, in London, said however that past experience showed that on key issues the Communists oftened opted out of voting, effectively giving the Socialists an absolute majority.
Muller said a key factor would be what positions the Communist party held in government. "Even if there are communists in government, they would be in minor positions."
Analysts said PIBOR contracts would probably be the hardest hit in the initial exchanges although the ultimate impact would depend very much on how well the franc held up against the mark.
Trading in French bond and interest-rate futures was due to start at 0500 GMT on Monday.

The French franc fell slightly after the initial projections showed an outright victory for the Socialists and then slipped to a low of 3.3835 per mark when later projections showed the Socialists would need the support of the Communists for a majority.
